summary: Tumor boards, recurring meetings at hospital institutions, assemble cancer specialists (e.g., medical oncology and pathology) to discuss patient care. In this work, we formally define tumor board case summarization, options generation, and meeting outcome prediction as AI tasks. We study datasets from four medical institutions and evaluate state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) from the DeepSeek, GPT, Gemini, and Qwen families using expert human assessment. Medical oncologists created ~9.6k reference texts and 16k human judgments across tasks. Clinicians rated LLM-generated case summaries 3.57–4.59 out of 5.0 across institutions, but recommendation generation remained more challenging, with average scores of 2.0–3.6. Clinical alignment analyses showed modest correlations of ~0.2 for case summarization subtasks and higher correlations of ~0.6 for recommendation generation using LLM-as-Judge metrics. Our proposed TBFact metrics were competitive with LLM-as-Judge approaches in longer prose free-text settings, suggesting a promising direction toward explainable evaluation. This study, to our knowledge the largest expert-grading study of tumor board tasks with both granular and direct assessments, found that criterion-level scores and overall judgments are related nonlinearly. Experts also frequently assigned high ratings to responses that differed substantially from their reference texts, challenging assumptions underlying reference-based automatic evaluation metrics.
title: Challenges in AI based tumor board case summarization and recommendations

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> AI is entering oncology workflows faster than evidence on stakeholder acceptance, trust, and sustained use. Existing syntheses rarely distinguish anticipated attitudes from actual use across oncology stakeholders. <strong>Objective:</strong> The aim of the study is to synthesize primary empirical evidence on stakeholder acceptance, trust, and implementation of AI in oncology and examine variation by stakeholder group, clinical task, AI exposure, and implementation maturity. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted a Joanna Briggs Institute–guided mixed methods systematic review with convergent integrated synthesis; the protocol was registered before formal eligibility screening. Eight databases were searched without date or language limits (August 6-9, 2026), yielding 46,206 records and 31,802 unique records. Title and abstract screening used 2 balanced primary allocations, joint bidirectional readjudication, and blinded verification of a stratified 10% (n=3182) sample. Full-text assessment, extraction, and critical appraisal were dual independent. Acceptance/Trust modes and F1-F8 coverage were independently coded across 309 studies and reconciled. Eight integrated findings were anchored to the nonadoption, abandonment, scale-up, spread, and sustainability framework; an emergent economic finding was reported separately. Adjusted stage models controlled for study design, publication format, and publication period; robustness analyses examined screening provenance and appraisal sensitivity. <strong>Results:</strong> We included 309 primary empirical studies; 187 (60.5%) were published in 2025 or 2026. Exposure ranged from hypothetical opinion to real-world implementation (n=82 studies), but only 6 described routine use. Acceptance was empirically assessed in 267 studies and Trust in 127. Relative to anticipatory stage 1, Acceptance assessment was less frequent in evaluated-interaction stage 2 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.07, 95% CI 0.02-0.25; <i>P</i><.001) and stages 3+4 (aOR 0.12, 95% CI 0.03-0.45; <i>P</i>=.001). Transparency/explainability coverage (F3) was lower in stages 3+4 (aOR 0.20, 95% CI 0.08-0.47; <i>q</i><0.001). Workflow/interoperability coverage (F5) was higher and governance coverage (F7) lower in both later contrasts after false discovery rate correction. Trust declined descriptively across stages, but adjusted contrasts were nonsignificant. Eight integrated findings spanned clinical value, performance, transparency, oversight, workflow, readiness, governance, and implementation, plus an emergent stage 1 economic finding. The principal Acceptance, F3, F5, and F7 findings persisted in the 229-study original screening subset. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> In oncology, the AI evidence profile appears to differ from anticipated use to implementation. Acceptance was empirically assessed most often before deployment; later-stage studies more often examined workflow and less often examined transparency and governance. The challenge is whether favorable attitudes and early deployment translate into calibrated, governed, and sustained routine use. An interpretive stage-specific model identifies assessment priorities across exposure and implementation contexts, but is not a validated causal or predictive model. Later-stage evaluations should retain measurement of Acceptance, trust calibration, governance, durability, and workflow outcomes. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> OSF Registries osf.io/nmep8; https://osf.io/nmep8
title: Stakeholder Acceptance, Trust, and Implementation of AI in Oncology: Mixed Methods Systematic Review

summary: Sexually transmitted infection (STI) diagnoses have increased in Britain since 2010, alongside major changes to sexual health policy, services, and disruptions owing to the COVID-19 pandemic. Meanwhile, sexual activity has decreased at population level, and more people report same-sex behaviours. To understand implications for HIV and STI control, we examined the general population prevalence of three STIs, sexual behaviours associated with STIs, and uptake of sexual health services, including HIV and chlamydia testing. We conducted the fourth National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4) between Sept 20, 2022, and April 5, 2024. In this analysis, we used cross-sectional data from 5949 sexually experienced (who reported ever having sex) participants aged 16-59 years in Britain from the probability sample surveys. We estimated weighted prevalences for STIs using biosamples (vaginal swabs or urine samples; n=2721), self-reported STI-associated behaviours (including a composite of ≥4 partners, condomless sex with ≥2 partners in the past year, or overlapping partners in the past 5 years), and sexual health service uptake. Comparisons were made between groups defined by partners' sex and over time by comparing with Natsal-3 (2010-12). In Natsal-4, overall prevalence of Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Trichomonas vaginalis was less than 1·0%. C trachomatis prevalence was highest in women aged 16-24 years (4·0%, 95% CI 1·3-11·7). STI-associated behaviours (composite) were most prevalent in young people (aged 16-24 years) with only opposite-sex partners (women 26·5%, 95% CI 20·2-33·9; men 29·4%, 22·5-37·6), women reporting sex with women and men (WSWM; 60·0%, 49·0-70·1), and men reporting sex with men (MSM; 57·1%, 48·6-65·3). Among those with only opposite-sex partners, past-year uptake was higher in women than men for sexual health service use (women 8·3%, 7·2-9·6; men 3·9%, 3·0-5·1), HIV testing (women 5·8%, 4·9-7·0; men 2·8%, 2·1-3·7), and chlamydia testing (women 8·4%, 7·1-10·1; men 4·7%, 3·4-6·4). Among participants reporting STI-associated behaviours, apart from MSM (47·3%, 36·1-58·8), the majority of people who reported STI-associated behaviours had not taken up services (eg, for sexual health services in participants with opposite-sex partners: women 73·8%, 67·8-79·1; men 84·9%, 79·4-89·4; WSWM 68·6%, 54.1-80.2). Between Natsal-3 and Natsal-4, HIV testing increased in MSM, sexual health service use decreased in young men with only opposite-sex partners, and chlamydia testing markedly declined (eg, in all women aged 16-24 years: Natsal-3 54·2%, 51·4-57·0; Natsal-4 17·8%, 12·7-24·5). Many people remain at behavioural risk for STIs, particularly young people, WSWM, and MSM. Most people with STI-associated behaviours had not used sexual health services in the past year. Declining chlamydia testing and high prevalence in young women might cause reproductive harm. Universal sexual health services remain essential. Wellcome Trust, Economic and Social Research Council, and the National Institute for Health and Care Research.
title: Sexually transmitted infections, behavioural risks, and uptake of sexual health services in Britain from 2010 to 2024: findings from the repeated cross-sectional National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal).

summary: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and cervical screening have substantially reduced overall cervical cancer risk, but differences in uptake must be quantified to inform equitable access. This study aimed to provide population-level evidence of the impact of HPV vaccination on HPV types 16 and 18 (hereafter HPV-16/18) prevalence in England, Scotland, and Wales (hereafter Britain), and uptake of cervical cancer prevention interventions (ie, vaccination and screening), 15 years after the introduction of the vaccination programme in 2008. We conducted the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), which are nationally representative, cross-sectional population surveys with individual-level data and HPV testing of biosamples. Data from Natsal-2 (1999-2001; before the vaccination programme was introduced, and included urine biosamples), Natsal-3 (2010-12; early in the vaccination programme, and included urine biosamples), and Natsal-4 (2022-24; after the vaccination programme was established, and included vaginal swab and urine biosamples) were analysed. Age-adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) for HPV-16/18 infection were estimated among women eligible for routine vaccination (born from Sept 1, 1995) compared with same-aged women before the vaccination programme was introduced. Combined Natsal-4 probability and non-probability data assessed factors associated with self-reported HPV vaccination and cervical screening. Among 10 418 Natsal-4 women (aged 16-59 years), 1059 women in the probability sample group (aged 18-44 years) provided usable biosamples (Natsal-2 n=1849; Natsal-3 n=2407). HPV-16/18 prevalence was 86% lower (aPR 0·14, 95% CI 0·02-0·84) among those aged 18-29 years in Natsal-4 (1·6%, 95% CI 0·3-8·2) than in Natsal-2 (8·7%, 95% CI 6·7-11·3). All HPV-16/18 infections reported in Natsal-4 occurred in unvaccinated women. Of 733 routine vaccination-eligible women, 23·0% (95% CI 19·4-27·0) reported being unvaccinated. Among 3530 women (aged 25-59 years) eligible for cervical screening, 5·3% (95% CI 4·4-6·3) reported never attending screening. Non-uptake of vaccination and screening was higher among minority ethnic groups, religious groups, and those born outside the UK. Prevalence of high-risk, non-vaccine-preventable HPV (HPV 35, 39, 51, 56, and 59) infections was 4·9% (95% CI 3·7-6·4) in the total population, without any statistically significant differences between these subgroups. Women with higher-risk sexual behaviours were more likely to both be vaccinated and attend for screening. Britain's HPV vaccination programme has driven a dramatic decline in HPV-16/18 prevalence and WHO cervical cancer elimination targets might be achievable overall if this is sustained. However, women from minority ethnic groups, religious groups, and those not born in the UK are less likely to be vaccinated and screened while remaining at risk. It is crucial to improve the reach of prevention interventions to more equitably reduce cervical cancer morbidity and mortality. Wellcome Trust, Economic and Social Research Council, and the National Institute for Health Research.
title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, vaccination, and cervical screening in Britain from 1999 to 2024: findings from the repeated cross-sectional National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal).

summary:
Importance

Early treatment with antibiotics is considered an important intervention to reduce mortality for patients with sepsis.

Objective

To determine the effect of earlier treatment with antibiotics in the ambulance on 90-day mortality compared with usual treatment in the emergency department.

Design, setting, and participants

This multicenter, 2 × 2 factorial randomized, placebo-controlled trial was conducted among 4 paramedic services and their destination hospitals in Ontario, Canada. Participants were adults with suspected sepsis, defined as suspected infection, fever (≥38.0 °C), and hypotension (systolic blood pressure <100 mm Hg). Patients were enrolled between March 23, 2020, and August 20, 2025, with final follow-up in December 2025.

Interventions

Patients were randomized to receive 1 g of intramuscular ceftriaxone or placebo (and to receive liberal fluids vs usual fluids; reported separately) during prehospital care in the ambulance. All patients could receive open-label antibiotics in the emergency department.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was hospital mortality, defined as death prior to hospital discharge to day 90. There were 17 secondary outcomes, including all-cause mortality at 90 days, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, use of mechanical ventilation, use of dialysis, positive culture results, and antibiotics within 24 hours of hospital arrival.

Results

Among 2091 randomized patients, 2048 were eligible for the primary analysis, with 1026 randomized to receive ceftriaxone and 1022 randomized to receive placebo. The median (IQR) age of patients was 75 (62-85) years and 1162 (56.7%) were males. The mean (SD) time from paramedic arrival at patient to administration of study drug was 37 (36) minutes in the ceftriaxone group and 39 (55) minutes in the placebo group. Most patients (735 of 795 [92.5%] in the ceftriaxone group and 730 of 792 [92.2%] in placebo group) were treated with antibiotics in the hospital after a mean (SD) of 247.3 (207.7) minutes after paramedic arrival among patients in the ceftriaxone group and 252.8 (218.0) minutes among the placebo group. The rate of hospital mortality was 182 of 1009 (18.0%) in the ceftriaxone group and 186 of 1011 (18.4%) in the placebo group (risk ratio, 0.97 [95% CI, 0.81-1.17]; P = .77). Of 17 secondary outcomes, all were similar between the groups.

Conclusions and relevance

Among patients with suspected sepsis on evaluation by paramedics, earlier treatment with antibiotics in the ambulance did not reduce mortality compared with usual care provided in the emergency department.

summary: The current less intensive guidelines for pulmonary nodule follow-up have not been compared with more intensive strategies. To determine whether less intensive follow-up of small pulmonary nodules is noninferior to more intensive follow-up. Unblinded, cluster randomized, pragmatic comparative effectiveness trial. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02623712). 24 clusters of U.S. hospitals and health care systems. 34 686 patients with a new pulmonary nodule measuring 15 mm or less, detected incidentally or by screening. Follow-up protocols were modeled on current and prior recommendations from the Fleischner Society and the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS). Each cluster was randomly assigned to the less or more intensive follow-up protocol. The primary outcome was the proportion of lung cancers measuring more than 20 mm at diagnosis. Analyses were conducted using mixed-effects logistic regression. The prespecified noninferiority margin was 5 percentage points. A total of 34 686 participants (50.8% women) were enrolled, with a mean age of 64.5 years (SD, 11.7). Lung cancer was diagnosed within 27 months of nodule identification in 273 of 17 841 participants (1.5%) in the less intensive group and 231 of 16 845 (1.4%) in the more intensive group. Among participants with lung cancer with available data, 97 of 267 (36.3%) in the less intensive group and 62 of 224 (27.7%) in the more intensive group had cancers larger than 20 mm at diagnosis. After adjustment, more lung cancers larger than 20 mm were identified with less intensive screening (7 percentage points [95% CI, -2.0 to 15.9 percentage points]), exceeding the noninferiority margin but not statistically significant. Suboptimal adherence, limited power, and residual confounding. Small, malignant pulmonary nodules frequently progress during follow-up. Although neither follow-up strategy was clearly superior, these data raise concerns about the less intensive recommendations for follow-up of small nodules. title: Less Versus More Intensive Strategies for Follow-up of Small Pulmonary Nodules : A Cluster Randomized Pragmatic Clinical Trial.

summary: Pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are prevalent and potential precursors of pancreatic cancer. Cancer risk assessment is a crucial step in PCL management, but the complexity and limited accuracy of existing approaches contribute to suboptimal patient care. We developed and validated an artificial intelligence (AI) model that uses radiology reports and clinical data to predict the future risk of pancreatic cancer in patients with PCLs. The model was developed and tested in a 13-year retrospective cohort comprising 23,398 abdominal CT/MRI examination reports from 8707 patients with PCLs across a multisite healthcare system. Of these, 430 (1.8%) corresponded to patients who later developed pancreatic cancer, defined as adenocarcinoma, invasive mucinous neoplasm, or high-grade dysplasia. Among the models evaluated, XGBoost achieved the highest performance, with AUCs of 0.960, 0.945, and 0.944 for predicting pancreatic cancer incidence at 1, 3, and 5 years after imaging, respectively. The model outperformed guideline-based risk stratification, with AUC improvements of 0.161 to 0.235 (P < 0.001). For examinations conducted within a year before cancer diagnosis, radiologists identified potential cancer in 51.5% of cases, while the AI model flagged 82.3%. These findings support the potential of AI to complement existing approaches for individualized pancreatic cancer risk stratification in patients with PCLs.
title: Artificial intelligence model for pancreatic cancer risk prediction in patients with pancreatic cystic lesions

summary:
Importance

Acute behavioral disturbance is a high-risk emergency department presentation. There is limited evidence for the comparative effectiveness of intramuscular sedative medications in children and adolescents, which may be required when there is imminent risk of serious harm due to agitation.

Objective

To determine whether olanzapine is more effective than droperidol intramuscularly in achieving behavioral containment.

Design, setting, and participants

This investigator-initiated, open-label, multicenter, superiority, randomized clinical trial recruited children and adolescents aged 9 to 17 years presenting to 10 Australian emergency departments with acute behavioral disturbance clinically deemed to require intramuscular medication from November 8, 2021, to February 16, 2026. The last participant follow-up occurred on March 17, 2026. Data were analyzed from April 15 to 27, 2026.

Interventions

Participants were randomly assigned to a single weight-based dose of olanzapine or droperidol (<40 kg, 5 mg; ≥40 kg, 10 mg).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was successful sedation (Sedation Assessment Tool score ≤0) without the need for additional sedatives 1 hour after randomization. A range of secondary outcomes, including adverse events, were assessed.

Results

Of 348 recruited individuals (mean [IQR] age, 14.9 [13.6-16.1] years; 215 [62%] female; 75 Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander individuals), 176 were assigned to olanzapine and 172 to droperidol. Of those randomized, 117 individuals (66%) in the olanzapine group and 121 individuals (70%) in the droperidol group were administered their study medication within 30 minutes of randomization. Successful sedation without the requirement for additional sedatives occurred in 89 individuals (53%) in the olanzapine group and 104 individuals (62%) in the droperidol group. No evidence of superiority was observed (adjusted risk difference, -8.3% [95% CI, -18.6% to 2.1%]; P = .12). One serious adverse event (apnea) occurred in the olanzapine group.

Conclusions and relevance

In this randomized clinical trial in children and adolescents presenting to the emergency department with behavioral disturbance, intramuscular olanzapine did not result in a clinically meaningfully greater proportion achieving successful sedation compared with droperidol. The limited effectiveness observed with both medications highlights the need for more effective pharmacological and nonpharmacological management strategies.

summary: Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) is a B cell maturation-antigen-targeting chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell product approved for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma treatment. Previously reported cases of post-cilta-cel immune effector cell enterocolitis (IEC-EC) have been described as a severe diarrhea associated with clonal CAR T cell populations. Here we report nine cases of cilta-cel-associated IEC-EC with CAR T cell-positive (CAR+) infiltration in 158 cilta-cel-treated patients at MD Anderson Cancer Center (incidence of 5.1% at a 6-month landmark and 5.7% globally). Cilta-cel infiltration was the primary cause of IEC-EC, and all cases demonstrated monoclonal or oligoclonal T cell populations as measured by vector integration analysis, flow cytometry and T cell receptor sequencing. Patients with IEC-EC had 100-fold more CAR T cell persistence in the peripheral blood than patients without IEC-EC. RNA sequencing analysis revealed increased cytotoxic and inflammatory programs associated with the CAR+ infiltrates relative to controls. Clonal vector integration occurred in introns of highly expressed genes without evidence of vector-mediated mutagenesis. Candidate driver mutations were sparse and heterogeneous, distinguishing IEC-EC from peripheral T cell lymphoma following CAR T cell therapy. In sum, we find that IEC-EC pathology represents a distinct, duodenum-predominant, clonal lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by the infiltration of clonal CAR+ cytotoxic T cells into the gastrointestinal tract. Multimodal profiling of patients with biopsy-confirmed immune effector cell-associated enterocolitis following ciltacabtagene autoleucel shows that CAR T cell infiltrates are concentrated in the duodenum and have a more cytotoxic and clonal phenotype with loss of resident T cells, suggesting that this is a lymphoproliferative disorder with neoplastic characteristics.

summary:
Background

The R21/Matrix-M (R21) malaria vaccine candidate, recommended by WHO for use in young children, could be extended to the whole population. Seasonal mass vaccination (SMV) before peak malaria transmission could be a promising tool to accelerate progress towards malaria elimination. We aimed to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of SMV with R21 in two malaria-endemic settings in west Africa.

Methods

This open-label, cluster-randomised, controlled trial was conducted in The Gambia, a setting with low-to-moderate seasonal transmission, and Burkina Faso, a setting with intense seasonal transmission. 54 medium-sized villages (30 in The Gambia and 24 in Burkina Faso) were randomly assigned (1:1) by use of computer-restricted randomisation to receive either SMV with R21 (intervention group) or no SMV (control group). All study villages received national standard malaria control interventions. In the intervention group, residents who were aged 5 months and older, willing to comply with trial procedures, and could provide written informed consent (from parents or guardians for children aged <18 years plus assent for children aged 12-17 years) were eligible for vaccination. The intervention was delivered as three monthly doses of 5 μg (participants aged <15 years) or 10 μg (participants aged ≥15 years) R21 plus 50 μg of Matrix-M. The primary outcome was malaria prevalence at peak transmission, defined as the proportion of participants with Plasmodium falciparum infection assessed by quantitative PCR. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06578572) and the Pan-African Clinical Trials Registry (PACTR202404544467702), and is ongoing.

Findings

The intervention was delivered between May 30, and Aug 21, 2024. A cross-sectional survey to estimate the primary endpoint was conducted between Nov 18 and Dec 6, 2024. The population available for vaccination varied across the three rounds. In The Gambia, among 4311 total residents in intervention villages, 2565 (59·5%) received three vaccine doses; in Burkina Faso, among 6235 total residents in intervention villages, 4072 (65·3%) received three vaccine doses. SMV with R21 reduced the odds of malaria infection by 70% (adjusted odds ratio 0·30 [95% CI 0·20-0·44]; p<0·0001) in The Gambia and by 25% (0·75 [95% CI 0·58-0·98]; p=0·036) in Burkina Faso. In The Gambia, prevalence decreased across all age groups, whereas in Burkina Faso the largest effect was observed in children younger than 5 years. The vaccine was safe and well tolerated. 651 adverse events were reported in 581 (13·5%) vaccine recipients in The Gambia, and 795 adverse events were reported in 705 (11·3%) vaccine recipients in Burkina Faso. Among 69 serious adverse events reported overall, only one was considered related to vaccination (febrile convulsions in a female participant aged 8 years after the second dose in The Gambia).

Interpretation

SMV with R21 reduced malaria prevalence in both settings. It could become an additional strategy for malaria control in endemic areas of seasonal transmission. In low-to-moderate transmission settings, the vaccine could accelerate progress towards elimination; in high-transmission areas it could further reduce the malaria burden.

UK Medical Research Council and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office.
title: Seasonal mass vaccination with R21/Matrix-M against malaria in The Gambia and Burkina Faso: an open-label, cluster-randomised, controlled trial.

summary:
Importance

Ionizing radiation from medical imaging may increase brain tumor risk.

Objective

To quantify brain tumor risk associated with radiation exposure from medical imaging in children and adolescents.

Design, setting, and participants

Retrospective cohort study of children born from 1996 through 2016 who were enrolled from birth in 6 US health care systems or Ontario, Canada, and were alive and cancer-free at age 2 years, with follow-up through December 31, 2017 (US sites), and December 31, 2024 (Ontario).

Exposures

Cumulative radiation dose to the brain from medical imaging, lagged by 2 years.

Main outcomes and measures

Incident brain or other central nervous system tumors. Hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models for categorical dose, and excess relative risks (ERRs) were estimated using linear dose-response models for continuous dose.

Results

Among 3 704 860 children (1 900 285 [51.3%] male) followed up for 45 671 641 person-years (mean follow-up, 12.3 years), 1536 brain tumors were diagnosed. Mean radiation dose from 1 head computed tomography (CT) examination was 66.2 mGy (SD, 22.2). Among children with cumulative dose of 1 mGy or greater, mean cumulative dose was 73 mGy (SD, 95) overall and 100 mGy (SD, 105) among those diagnosed with brain tumors. Compared with no exposure, brain tumor risk increased with cumulative dose (>0 to <1 mGy: HR, 1.12 [95% CI, 1.01-1.26]; 1 to <5 mGy: HR, 1.71 [95% CI, 0.88-2.96]; 5 to <50 mGy: HR, 1.86 [95% CI, 1.16-2.81]; 50 to <75 mGy: HR, 2.30 [95% CI, 1.64-3.12]; 75 to <100 mGy: HR, 2.02 [95% CI, 1.13-3.30]; 100 to <150 mGy: HR, 2.81 [95% CI, 1.53-4.66]; ≥150 mGy: HR, 3.85 [95% CI, 2.43-5.75]). Cumulative dose was associated with brain tumor risk overall (ERR per 100 mGy, 1.27 [95% CI, 0.83-1.77]; P < .001), with stronger associations for aggressive histologies (ERR per 100 mGy, 1.51 [95% CI, 1.00-2.11]; P < .001). By age 21 years, exposure comparable to 1 head CT was associated with 7.9 excess brain tumors per 10 000 children, or approximately 1 excess tumor per 1266 head CT examinations. The estimated population-attributable fraction was 10.1% (95% CI, 5.8%-14.2%).

Conclusions and relevance

summary: The risk of developing dementia at any given age has fallen steadily in Europe and the United States over recent decades. A key unresolved question is whether recent generations reach older age with better cognitive capacity, experience slower cognitive decline, or both, as this has implications for when preventive interventions are likely to have the greatest impact. Analyzing ~783,000 episodic-memory assessments from ~219,000 individuals in five longitudinal studies followed for up to 30 years, we find that later-born generations benefit from a double dividend, with higher memory levels entering old age and slower decline thereafter. The combined advantage is large enough to plausibly account for the reported 13% per-decade decline in dementia incidence. Improvements are concentrated among the fastest decliners; later-born generations show longer periods of stable memory, and their slower decline is mirrored by lower rates of clinical impairment and slower hippocampal atrophy. Calendar-time trends affecting all generations simultaneously are unlikely to explain these differences. Because memory level is built mainly in early life whereas the rate of decline is shaped by conditions in adulthood, sustaining the decline in dementia incidence will require prevention policies that protect brain health across the whole lifespan, beginning in childhood. A study of longitudinal cohorts from Europe and the United States over 30 years showed that later-born generations benefit from higher cognitive capacity and memory stability, which may explain the trend of declining dementia incidence rates.

summary: Medicare Shared Savings Program Accountable Care Organizations Performance Year 2025 Financial and Quality Results Medicare Shared Savings Program (Shared Savings Program) Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are critical in helping Make America Healthy Again — by supporting high-quality, coordinated care that addresses prevention, chronic illness and the root causes of disease. The Shared Savings Program’s unique design means ACOs are held accountable for saving money and improving healthcare quality, delivering a win for both patients and the Medicare Trust Funds. The Shared Savings Program is one of the largest programs in the country that aims to reduce overall costs of care while ensuring Medicare beneficiaries receive high-quality care. For Performance Year (PY) 2025, ACOs in the Shared Savings Program achieved the highest rates of shared savings since the inception of the program. Out of 472 ACOs, 80% of ACOs, representing 84% of the 10.9 million assigned beneficiaries, are earning performance payments totaling $4.9 billion, and Medicare saved $2.5 billion relative to benchmarks. PY 2025 had the highest share of ACOs receiving performance payments and the highest amount of savings for ACOs and Medicare since the inception of the Shared Savings Program. Financial Results ACOs had higher gross per capita savings in PY 2025 compared to PY 2024, $690 vs $643, respectively. However, ACOs had lower net per capita savings in PY 2025 compared to PY 2024, $234 vs $241. The decrease in net per capita savings represents more ACOs moving into two-sided risk tracks (a 4 percentage point increase between PY 2024 and PY 2025), and ACOs participating in two-sided tracks are eligible for higher shared savings rates and, therefore, can retain more of the savings they earned. Gross per capita savings are the savings shared by ACOs and Medicare, whereas net per capita savings represent the savings for Medicare only. Low revenue ACOs continue to outperform high revenue ACOs, generating $300 vs $169 net per capita savings. Typically, low revenue ACOs are physician-led ACOs or are comprised of federally qualified health centers and/or rural health centers, while high revenue ACOs are hospital-led. Additionally, ACOs composed predominantly of primary care clinicians had higher performance compared to ACOs with fewer primary care clinicians, with $417 vs $208 in net per capita savings. In its first PY (PY 2025), the 24 ACOs participating in the CMS Innovation Center’s ACO Primary Care Flex (ACO PC Flex) model generated $652 in gross per capita savings and $186 in net per capita savings. Notably, 92% of PC Flex ACOs (22 of 24) earned shared savings, compared with ~80% of all Shared Savings Program ACOs. The difference between gross and net per capita savings reflects, in part, that 88% of PC Flex ACOs participate under the ENHANCED track, which offers the highest shared savings rate, and that 33% of PC Flex ACOs are new ACOs. The ACO PC Flex model has a Prospective Primary Care (PPC) Payment option to shift payment for primary care away from fee-for-service, visit-based payment to a flexible, predictable revenue stream. PC Flex ACOs also performed well on quality measures, comparable to similar Shared Savings Program ACOs. Twenty-nine eligible ACOs received advance investment payments (AIPs), intended to provide advanced shared savings for upfront investments to build the infrastructure needed to succeed in the Shared Savings Program and address beneficiary needs. Twenty-five AIP ACOs shared in savings totaling $46 million, and as part of this financial reconciliation cycle, we will recoup $22 million of these advance payments from AIP ACOs that earned shared savings. ACOs that achieved savings had lower utilization compared to their benchmark across many categories of utilization including hospital discharges, Emergency Department (ED) Visits, number of Skilled Nursing Facility (SNF) stays, and SNF Utilization Days. Thirteen ACOs owed shared losses totaling $23 million. Quality Results All ACOs reported the new Alternative Payment Model (APM) Performance Pathway (APP) Plus quality measure set in PY 2025 and met quality reporting requirements under the Shared Savings Program. Adoption of all-payer digital quality measures (electronic clinical quality measures [eCQMs]) and Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) clinical quality measures (CQMs) also increased from PY 2024. CMS continues to encourage ACOs to move toward reporting digital quality measures using electronically stored and transmitted health information, leveraging interoperability, reducing burden, and improving efficiency. Medicare Clinical Quality Measures for ACOs participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Medicare CQMs) became the most commonly reported collection type in PY 2025. Additionally, 264 ACOs reported at least one Medicare CQM in PY 2025, compared to 64 ACOs in PY 2024. ACOs that reported Medicare CQMs in both PYs 2024 and 2025 showed significant improvement on measures of controlling blood pressure, glycemic status assessments, and rates of depression screening with a follow-up plan. Shared Savings Program ACOs helped more patients improve markers of good health, such as controlled blood pressure and diabetes management, compared to 2024. Among ACOs that reported quality measures as eCQMs, the mean percentage of beneficiaries with adequately controlled high blood pressure increased significantly from PY 2024 to PY 2025 (from 71.21% to 73.86%). Among ACOs that reported eCQMs, the mean percentage of beneficiaries with poorly controlled diabetes (glycemic status assessment greater than 9%) declined significantly from PY 2024 to PY 2025 (from 28.36% to 24.63%). Nearly all ACOs outperformed similar types of physician groups on quality measures: ACOs performed significantly better than comparable physician groups on eCQMs for Screening for Depression and Follow-up Plan (55.03% among ACOs versus 50.64% among comparable MIPS groups) and Controlling High Blood Pressure (73.86% among ACOs versus 70.38% among comparable MIPS groups). ACOs have performed consistently better than comparable physician groups on the patient experience survey measure, Getting Timely Care, Appointments, and Information for every year that the survey has been fielded since 2019. Calendar Year 2027 Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule Updates The Trump Administration is committed to ensuring that ACOs’ participation in the Shared Savings Program promotes better chronic disease management and prevention, more efficient use of resources and innovation, and drives increased savings for the Medicare Trust Funds. To advance these goals, in the Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) Final Rule released on Nov. 4, 2026, and effective Jan. 1, 2027, CMS finalized policies that will strengthen incentives for ACOs to join and remain in the program, expand accountable care relationships for beneficiaries, improve the accuracy of financial benchmarks and beneficiary assignment, reduce administrative burden, and advance digital quality measurement and interoperability. Among these policies, the creation of a new growth adjustment to the historical benchmark will create a financial incentive for ACOs to recruit providers who are new to Medicare shared savings initiatives and serve beneficiaries who have not previously participated in accountable care relationships. These policies also provide opportunities to increase shared savings payments; ACOs in level E of the BASIC track will see their shared savings rate increase from 50% to 60%, and ACOs that already generate strong savings through the prior savings adjustment will have opportunities to increase shared savings payments with the prior savings adjustment’s scaling factor increasing from 50% to 75%. Additionally, starting Jan. 1, 2027, ACO-participating clinicians will have the option to receive higher payment for office visits with additional complexity, recognizing the added investments ACOs make in care coordination and giving clinicians a direct, meaningful financial incentive to join or remain in an ACO. CMS is also updating our beneficiary assignment policies to expand the number of beneficiaries eligible for the Shared Savings Program, while reducing gaming opportunities. Additionally, CMS is finalizing changes to the quality reporting requirements to: extend availability of a MIPS CQM collection type and extend the associated MIPS CQM reporting incentive, extend the use of flat benchmarks to score Medicare CQMs, revise the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirement to allow ACOs to exclude ACO Participant TIN(s) from the ACO’s quality data submission under certain circumstances, revise the definition of a beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs to align with an ACO’s assigned beneficiary population, establish the Medicare eCQMs collection type to further support ACOs in the transition to dQM reporting, revise the Shared Savings Program scoring policy for excluded measures or measures that lack a benchmark, halt plans for ACOs to report more quality measures, and simplify Shared Savings Program certified electronic health record technology (CEHRT) use requirements. Lastly, Shared Savings Program ACOs, for the first time, will have the option to reduce or eliminate beneficiary cost sharing for certain Part B services, giving ACOs a direct, tangible benefit to offer the patients they serve and strengthening the beneficiary engagement case for healthcare providers joining or starting an ACO. Background

Childhood obesity is a chronic, neurometabolic disease with limited options for medical treatments that are efficacious and durable. Once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide is approved for the treatment of obesity in adolescents and adults, but data for its use in young children are lacking.

Methods

We conducted a phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving children (6 to <12 years of age) with obesity. Participants were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide or placebo for a period of 104 weeks, after which participants stopped taking semaglutide or placebo for a 7-week washout period. Both groups received counseling for lifestyle modification. The primary end point was the percent change in the body-mass index (BMI; the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) from baseline to week 68. The confirmatory secondary end point was a reduction in BMI category at week 68.

Results

Among 167 children who underwent randomization, 112 were assigned to receive semaglutide and 55 to receive placebo. At week 68, the mean percent change in BMI was -13.5% with semaglutide and 2.7% with placebo (estimated between-group difference, -16.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -19.4 to -12.9; P<0.001). The percent change in BMI at week 104 was -9.4% with semaglutide and 8.4% with placebo (between-group difference, -17.8 percentage points; 95% CI, -22.2 to -13.3). At week 68, a reduction in BMI category had occurred in 79% of the participants in the semaglutide group and in 23% of those in the placebo group (odds ratio, 7.8; 95% CI, 3.5 to 17.6; P<0.001), with the BMI below the threshold for obesity (the 95th percentile for age and sex) in 38% of the participants who received semaglutide and in 2% of those who received placebo. Adverse events occurred in 96% of the participants receiving semaglutide and in 93% of those receiving placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common, occurred more frequently with semaglutide than with placebo, and led to discontinuation in 1 participant in the semaglutide group.

Conclusions

Among children (6 to <12 years of age) with obesity, treatment with semaglutide for 68 weeks resulted in a significantly greater mean percent reduction in BMI than placebo. (Funded by Novo Nordisk; STEP Young ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05726227.).

summary:
Importance

Obesity is a major health problem in China; more pharmacotherapy choices for long-term weight management are needed.

Objective

To evaluate the efficacy and safety of once-weekly subcutaneous ribupatide, a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, for weight loss in adults in China with overweight or obesity without diabetes.

Design, setting, and participants

This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 clinical trial was conducted at 55 sites in China. From May to June 2024, adults without diabetes who had a body mass index of 28 or greater or 24 or greater with at least 1 weight-related comorbidity were enrolled, with final follow-up on June 20, 2025.

Interventions

Participants were randomized to receive once-weekly subcutaneous ribupatide (target doses of 2 mg, 4 mg, or 6 mg) or matching placebo for 48 weeks, with dose escalation for up to 20 weeks and concomitant lifestyle intervention.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was change in body weight from baseline to week 48, including percent change in body weight and the percentage of participants achieving at least 5% body weight reduction, analyzed under the treatment policy estimand.

Results

Among 567 randomized participants (309 [54.5%] female; mean [SD] age was 34.4 [8.4] years, body weight was 93.0 [17.3] kg, and body mass index was 33.3 [4.5]), 514 (90.7%) completed the 48-week treatment period. Least-squares mean percentage changes in body weight at week 48 were -10.7%, -16.4%, and -17.7% with ribupatide 2, 4, and 6 mg, respectively, vs -1.4% with placebo. At week 48, the placebo-adjusted differences in percentage change in body weight were -9.3 (95% CI, -11.4 to -7.3) percentage points with ribupatide 2 mg, -15.0 (95% CI, -17.1 to -12.9) percentage points with ribupatide 4 mg, and -16.3 (95% CI, -18.4 to -14.2) percentage points with ribupatide 6 mg (P < .001 for all). For at least 5% body weight reduction at week 48, the multiply imputed response rates were 68.1% (95% CI, 59.9% to 75.3%) for ribupatide 2 mg (97 of 142), 88.0% (95% CI, 81.3% to 92.6%) for ribupatide 4 mg (124 of 141), 85.7% (95% CI, 78.6% to 90.7%) with ribupatide 6 mg (121 of 141), and 16.0% (95% CI, 10.8% to 23.1%) with placebo (23 of 143). Placebo-adjusted differences for ribupatide 2, 4, and 6 mg were 52.0 (95% CI, 42.2 to 61.9), 72.0 (95% CI, 63.7 to 80.2), and 69.7 (95% CI, 61.1 to 78.3) percentage points, respectively (all P < .001). The most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events with ribupatide were gastrointestinal events, occurring in 47.9%, 58.2%, and 63.1% of participants receiving ribupatide 2 mg, 4 mg, and 6 mg, respectively, compared with 23.1% receiving placebo; most were mild to moderate in severity and few participants (0.7%) permanently discontinued study treatment because of adverse events.

Conclusions and relevance

Among adults in China with overweight or obesity without diabetes, once-weekly subcutaneous ribupatide resulted in significantly greater weight loss at 48 weeks. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent tolerability findings.

summary:
Importance

Information on the effects of tirzepatide, a once-weekly glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist approved for obesity management in adults with obesity, remains limited in adolescents.

Objective

To evaluate the efficacy and safety of once-weekly tirzepatide in adolescents with obesity or overweight with at least 1 obesity-related complication.

Design, setting, and participants

This phase 3, randomized, double-blind, 72-week clinical trial was conducted at 31 medical research centers and hospitals in Canada, the Czech Republic, Israel, Italy, Poland, and the US from October 16, 2023, to June 2, 2026, among adolescents aged 12 years to younger than 18 years with obesity or overweight with at least 1 obesity-related complication.

Interventions

Participants were randomized 2:1 to receive once-weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide, escalated to a maximum tolerated dose (5, 10, or 15 mg), or placebo for 72 weeks, in addition to healthy lifestyle intervention.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary end point was percent change in body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) from baseline to week 72. Key secondary end points included percentages of participants achieving BMI reductions of at least 5%, at least 10%, at least 15%, and at least 20%; changes in BMI SD score; BMI expressed as a percentage of the 95th percentile; and body weight, waist circumference, and physical functioning from baseline to week 72. Safety outcomes included treatment-emergent adverse events, serious adverse events, and discontinuations due to adverse events.

Results

A total of 160 participants were randomized to receive tirzepatide (n = 109) or placebo (n = 51). Mean (SD) age at baseline was 14.6 (1.6) years, 99 participants (61.9%) were female, mean body weight was 109.7 kg, and mean BMI was 38.6. At week 72, tirzepatide was associated with 18.5% reduction in BMI, compared with 0.5% increase in BMI with placebo, demonstrating superiority over placebo (estimated treatment difference, -19.0 [95% CI, -23.9 to -14.1] percentage points; P < .001). Of 10 key secondary outcomes, all demonstrated statistically significant differences favoring tirzepatide compared with placebo. Overall, 79.6% of tirzepatide-treated participants achieved BMI reduction of at least 5% compared with 28.5% of participants in the placebo group (risk difference, 51.2 [95% CI, 36.3-66.1] percentage points; P < .001). The most common adverse events with tirzepatide treatment were gastrointestinal (mostly mild to moderate).

Conclusions and relevance

In adolescents with obesity or overweight with obesity-related complications, tirzepatide, in addition to healthy lifestyle intervention, led to significant reductions in percent change in BMI compared with placebo at 72 weeks.
